title: Counting simple polygonalizations
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given a finite planar point set \(S\subset\mathbb Q^2\) in binary rational coordinates, outputs the exact number \(\operatorname{poly}(S)\) of simple polygonalizations of \(S\)?

A simple polygonalization is a non-self-intersecting closed polygonal curve that visits every point of \(S\) exactly once and joins consecutive points by straight segments. Two cyclic orders count as the same polygonalization precisely when one is obtained from the other by changing the starting point or reversing the traversal. Collinear points are allowed, but crossings, overlapping edges and contacts between nonadjacent edges are forbidden.

The running time must be polynomial in the total binary input length, including the coordinate encodings, and the output count is written in binary.
why: This is a basic exact-counting question for a geometric family of Hamiltonian cycles. A resolution would clarify whether planarity of the drawing and freedom to choose its edges make counting fundamentally easier than familiar hard graph-counting problems, and would separate compact numerical output from exhaustive geometric enumeration.
status_note: Source-open in TOPP Problem 16, revised 18 June 2025, and retained as unresolved counting complexity in Eppstein, Algorithmica 86 (2024), introduction and §6. On 16 September 2026, this review checked the 2016 published extended abstract’s general-position assumption and Hamilton-cycle theorem, and the full 2024 article’s enumeration model and counting discussion. Bounded 2025–2026 searches found no polynomial exact-counting algorithm or unconditional impossibility theorem for this target. This records dated explicit openness and limited later review, not an exhaustive current-status certification; the omitted full-version proofs behind the 2016 extended abstract were not independently audited.

progress.text: The original TOPP entry poses polynomial-time counting and records related monotone-polygon and random-generation work.
Marx and Miltzow obtain \(n^{O(\sqrt{n})}\)-time counting for noncrossing Hamilton cycles under their general-position assumption.

Eppstein obtains output-polynomial enumeration, including degenerate point sets, and polynomial-time estimates for the logarithm of the count. The published conclusion still asks about exact counting hardness.
The revised TOPP entry retains the polynomial-time counting question as open while adding the subexponential result.

importance.reason: A longstanding and repeatedly studied counting problem in computational geometry, with recent progress on subexponential algorithms and enumeration but no settled polynomial-time classification. It tests the algorithmic power of noncrossing geometry in a broadly recognizable family rather than optimizing one construction.

sentences: A simple polygonalization connects all points of a planar set into one noncrossing closed polygon.
The question asks whether its exact number can be computed in deterministic polynomial time from binary rational coordinates.
Starting-point changes and reverse traversals count as the same polygon, and collinear input points are allowed.
Subexponential counting in general position and output-polynomial enumeration are known, but neither gives a polynomial-time exact count for every input.
The problem tests whether geometric noncrossing structure can make a large family of Hamiltonian cycles efficiently countable.

definitions:
The input is a finite list \(S=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\) of pairwise distinct points \(p_i=(x_i,y_i)\in\mathbb Q^2\). Each rational coordinate is represented by a signed integer numerator and a positive integer denominator in binary, in lowest terms, using a fixed self-delimiting encoding. Let \(N\) be the total length in bits of the encoded list, including the coordinates, signs, delimiters and list length. Input order supplies labels for describing cyclic orders; it does not change the answer. The exact bit model makes the source’s polynomial-time question explicit rather than treating arbitrary-precision arithmetic as a unit-cost operation.

For \(n\ge3\), choose a permutation \((i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its edges are the closed segments
\[e_j=[p_{i_j},p_{i_{j+1}}],\qquad j=0,\ldots,n-1,\]
where indices are read modulo \(n\). Each edge must have no point of \(S\) in its relative interior. Two adjacent edges must intersect in exactly their common endpoint. Two nonadjacent edges must be disjoint. These conditions say that the cyclic polygonal curve is simple: it is an embedded circle made of line segments. In particular, edges cannot cross, overlap along a segment, or touch a nonincident vertex.

Three successive vertices may be collinear if the path proceeds straight through the middle vertex. Such an input point is still counted as a vertex even though its interior angle is \(\pi\). Reversing direction along an already traversed segment is forbidden by the intersection conditions. No general-position promise is imposed, and an arbitrary perturbation that changes collinearities would change the input counting problem.

A polygonalization uses every point and no additional vertices. Its region need not be convex, and its boundary need not be monotone in any direction. There is no prescribed graph of allowed edges, no obstacle polygon, no additional forbidden region and no weight or length objective. Admissibility depends only on the geometry of the given points and the straight segments selected between them.

Cyclic permutations of a valid order and reversal of that order describe one unoriented polygonalization. Distinct geometric edge sets on the fixed point set are counted separately, even if a symmetry of the point set maps one to another. For example, one can count each polygon exactly once using the representative with \(i_0=1\) and \(i_1<i_{n-1}\). These conventions remove the \(2n\)-fold starting-point and orientation multiplicity; they do not quotient by translations, rotations or reflections of the input configuration.

Define \(\operatorname{poly}(S)\) as the number of valid equivalence classes of cyclic orders. For \(n<3\), set \(\operatorname{poly}(S)=0\). A set with all points on one line also has count zero. For \(n\ge3\), the elementary bound
\[0\le\operatorname{poly}(S)\le (n-1)!/2\]
shows that the binary count has \(O(n\log(n+1))\) bits, despite potentially having many polygonalizations. The target is the count for each input set, not the maximum or minimum number over all \(n\)-point sets.

The computational model is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite description, ordinary bit operations and no oracle or advice. All input parsing, exact geometric predicates, integer arithmetic and output writing are charged to the running time. The requested quantifiers are
\[\exists A\;\exists a\ge1\;\exists k\in\mathbb N\;\forall S:\quad A(S)=\operatorname{poly}(S),\qquad \operatorname{time}_A(S)\le a(N+1)^k.\]
The constants and exponent are independent of the number, positions and encoding lengths of the points. The machine may return zero on malformed inputs; it can check the encoding and pairwise distinctness in polynomial time. There is no restriction on workspace beyond that implied by the time bound.

The task requires the exact integer count in binary. An estimate with bounded relative error, an approximation to the logarithm of the count, or a random polygon is a different computational task. This card asks a yes-or-no question about existence of an exact-counting algorithm, rather than asking the solver for a numerical value of a single instance or an unrestricted approximation to a function.

Writing down every polygonalization may require exponentially many symbols. An enumeration algorithm whose time is polynomial in that whole output length therefore need not run in time polynomial in \(N\), even though the binary count is short. Likewise, generating one simple polygon or listing only a particular geometric subclass does not compute the required count.

For complexity context, \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of integer-valued functions counting accepting branches of polynomial-time nondeterministic machines. A canonical cyclic order is a polynomial-size witness here, and its segment-intersection conditions can be verified exactly in polynomial bit time, placing the count in this class. \(\mathrm{FP}\) denotes functions computable by a deterministic polynomial-time machine. A conditional hardness theorem would describe consequences of a polynomial algorithm; it would not by itself refute the algorithm’s existence without proving the relevant separation.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the stated uniform deterministic polynomial-bit-time exact-counting algorithm. A positive answer must establish correctness for every encoded finite rational point set, including collinearities and zero-count cases, and a single polynomial bound that includes arithmetic and output costs. A negative answer must prove that no such machine and polynomial bound exist. A #P-hardness result conditional on an unproved complexity separation is progress but does not by itself supply that unconditional refutation. A polynomial-time approximation, output-polynomial enumeration, a result only for general-position or convex-position sets, or a lower bound for one particular counting algorithm does not satisfy the full target.

source_formulation.text: TOPP Problem 16 asks whether the number of simple polygonalizations of a planar point set can be computed in polynomial time, defining a polygonalization as a simple polygon with exactly the given vertices. The card retains that exact-counting existence question and spells out binary rational input, collinearities and the removal of cyclic-order multiplicities.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of TOPP Problem 16; computational encoding and counting conventions are explicit

context_blocks.text: Finding one noncrossing polygon through a point set and counting all such polygons are different tasks. The latter asks whether a geometric restriction on Hamiltonian cycles permits efficient exact counting despite the large number of possible cyclic orders.

Marx and Miltzow give a subexponential algorithm for counting noncrossing Hamilton cycles on point sets in general position. Their Theorem 6 states a running time of \(n^{O(\sqrt{n})}\). This is substantial progress but is not a polynomial-time bound, and their stated general-position hypothesis must be retained.

The same paper gives a sharper constant in the exponent for counting triangulations. The TOPP progress paragraph compresses these statements too aggressively: this card does not attribute the triangulation constant to every graph family, nor does it treat a triangulation count as a polygonalization count.

Eppstein proves that all polygonalizations can be listed in time polynomial in the input size and the total output size, even when the input has collinearities. An exponential number of polygons still permits an exponential running time under that guarantee.

Eppstein’s polynomial-time estimates concern the logarithm of the number of polygonalizations. Such an estimate can allow a large multiplicative uncertainty in the count itself. The paper’s conclusion retains both stronger approximate counting and the #P-completeness question as open.

For points in convex position there is only one polygonalization, while other configurations have exponentially many. The difficulty lies in determining the exact count for arbitrary inputs, not in the bit length needed to write the resulting integer.

Uniform random generation on a fixed point set is a closely related theme in the source. Heuristic generation or a distribution that favors some polygons is not a counting algorithm, and no unconditional equivalence with the exact counting target is asserted here.
